a: queen mother
t: The queen mother or the rulers?
p: The Hebrew says 'the queen mother'; the Greek has 'the rulers'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and to the queen mother
readings.plain: queen mother

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (dynasteuousin)
readings.en: and to the rulers
readings.plain: rulers

why: The Hebrew gevirah, 'great lady', names the king's mother, who held an office at court (1 Kings 15:13). Nothing in the Greek requires a different Hebrew text, and it may have read the word as 'lords' or simply generalized. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The queen mother of Judah was Nehushta, mother of Jehoiachin, who was taken to Babylon with him in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8, 12, 15; Jeremiah 29:2). If verse 18 belongs to that crisis, 'the king and the queen mother' are the pair who surrendered. 4QJer-a does not preserve this verse.

a: Surely I will free you for good
t: The LORD's promise or Jeremiah's prayer?
p: The Greek turns the verse into a prayer of Jeremiah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (Qere)
readings.en: Surely I will set you free for good
readings.plain: Surely I will free you for good

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: So be it, Master, as they prosper
readings.plain: So be it, Master, while they prosper

why: The Greek verse is a prayer, with no 'The LORD said'. It is hard to tell whether the translator read a different Hebrew text or struggled with a very difficult one. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, which has the LORD speaking, and notes that the verse is uncertain.
b: The Hebrew verse is obscure at several points (see the note). 4QJer-a preserves only 15:1-2 in this chapter, so no scroll helps here.

a: I will make your enemies cross into a land you do not know
p: Another reading has the LORD make Judah serve its enemies, as in 17:4.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: I will make your enemies pass over
readings.plain: I will make your enemies cross into a land you do not know

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (katadoulosō se ... tois echthrois sou); compare the Masoretic Text of 17:4
readings.en: I will make you serve your enemies
readings.plain: I will make you serve your enemies in a land you do not know

why: The two Hebrew readings differ by one letter (resh and dalet). The second reading is what 17:4 has, in a verse the Greek lacks, so it may be the original here and have been repeated in 17:4, or a scribe may have copied 17:4 into 15:14. The Masoretic Text makes sense as it is, and the witnesses are split, so the Plain English Translation keeps it and gives the other reading here.

a: Your words were found, and I ate them
t: 'Found and eaten' or 'bring them to an end'?
p: The Greek attaches the line to the end of verse 15 and reads a different verb.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: Your words were found, and I ate them
readings.plain: Your words were found, and I ate them

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (synteleson autous)
readings.en: Bring them to an end
readings.plain: Bring them to an end

why: In the Greek, verse 15 ends 'I bear reproach from those who set aside your words; bring them to an end' and the sentence 'your word will be my joy' follows. This may reflect a Hebrew with the consonants of 'consume them' (a different division of the same letters), or a translator's choice; the Hebrew also has a Ketiv/Qere between 'words' and 'word' in this verse. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text.
b: No scroll preserves this verse (4QJer-a ends this chapter's preserved text at 15:2).

a: my loyal love and my compassion
p: The Greek has no 'my loyal love and my compassion'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the loyal love and the compassion
readings.plain: my loyal love and my compassion

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: The Greek says only 'I have taken my peace from this people', so the Hebrew adds 'the loyal love and the compassion'. No scroll preserves this verse. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. If the Greek has the earlier edition, the extra words were added to bring in the great words of the covenant (Exodus 34:6); if the Greek abridged, it cut them.

a: Great and small will die in this land. They will not be buried.
p: The Greek lacks 'Great and small will die in this land. They will not be buried.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: וּמֵתוּ גְדֹלִים וּקְטַנִּים בָּאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת לֹא יִקָּבֵרוּ
readings.en: Great and small will die in this land; they will not be buried
readings.plain: Great and small will die in this land. They will not be buried.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: The Greek goes straight from 16:5 to 'they will not cut themselves'. The clause repeats the unburied dead of 16:4, so it could have been added in the Hebrew, or dropped in the Greek's source or by the translator. No scroll preserves it. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: Judah's sin is written with an iron pen, with a flint point. It is cut into the tablet of their heart and into the horns of your altars,
p: The Greek has no 17:1-4. This is the first of four entries.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen
readings.plain: Judah's sin is written with an iron pen, with a flint point. It is cut into the tablet of their heart and into the horns of your altars,

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: The Greek goes from 16:21 to 17:5 with nothing between. Four verses missing from the Greek fit the pattern of the book: the Greek is a shorter edition than the Hebrew. Tov and Bogaert argue that the Greek translates an earlier, shorter edition and the verses were added in the longer Hebrew one; a minority hold that the Greek abridged. The verses repeat 15:13-14, which the Greek has, in a form that differs; the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. 4QJer-a does not preserve 17:1-7.

a: as their children remember their altars and their Asherah poles by the green trees, on the high hills.
p: Part of the passage 17:1-4 that the Greek lacks.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: as their children remember their altars
readings.plain: as their children remember their altars and their Asherah poles by the green trees, on the high hills.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: See the entry on 17:1. The Hebrew of this verse is unclear (the kaph can mean 'as' or 'while'), and the Greek's lack of it may be a sign that the verse was not smoothly joined. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: O my mountain in the open country! Your wealth and all your treasures I will hand over to be plundered, and your high places too, because of sin throughout your territory.
p: Part of the passage 17:1-4 that the Greek lacks.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: my mountain in the field, your wealth
readings.plain: O my mountain in the open country! Your wealth and all your treasures I will hand over to be plundered, and your high places too, because of sin throughout your territory.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: See the entry on 17:1. The verse is almost the same as 15:13, which the Greek has in a different form (it lacks 'not for a price'). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: You yourself will let go of the inheritance I gave you. I will make you serve your enemies in a land you do not know, for you have kindled a fire in my anger that will burn forever.
p: Part of the passage 17:1-4 that the Greek lacks.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: you will let go, even you, of your inheritance
readings.plain: You yourself will let go of the inheritance I gave you. I will make you serve your enemies in a land you do not know, for you have kindled a fire in my anger that will burn forever.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: See the entry on 17:1. This verse supplies the reading 'I will make you serve your enemies' that the Greek has at 15:14 (see there). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: Heat may come, and it sees nothing of it
t: Does the tree 'see' or 'fear' the heat?
p: The written text says 'fear' and the margin says 'see'; the Greek has 'fear'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (Qere, the reading marked in the margin)
readings.en: and he will not see when heat comes
readings.plain: Heat may come, and it sees nothing of it

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (Ketiv, the written text); Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (ou phobēthēsetai)
readings.en: and he will not fear
readings.plain: Heat may come, and it has no fear of it

why: The two Hebrew words differ by one letter (he). 'See' matches 17:6, where the shrub 'does not see good when it comes' and gives the poem a neat symmetry; 'fear' is the written text and the Greek's word. The Plain English Translation follows the marked reading and gives the other here. 4QJer-a preserves nothing visible of this clause.

a: More crooked than anything is the heart
p: The Greek reads 'deep' for 'crooked' and 'man' for 'incurable'. This is the first of two entries.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: The heart is crooked beyond everything
readings.plain: More crooked than anything is the heart

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (batheia)
readings.en: The heart is deep beyond everything
readings.plain: Deeper than anything is the heart

why: 'Deep' would be a different Hebrew word ('amoq), or the translator's guess for a hard word. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, with 'crooked'.
b: 4QJer-a has the second half of the verse ('beyond everything, and it is incurable/human. Who knows it?') in a damaged state: the word 'aqov is restored by the editors and not visible.

a: it is sick beyond healing
p: The Greek has 'and it is a man'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (written without a vowel letter, which fits either word)
readings.en: and it is incurable
readings.plain: it is sick beyond healing

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (kai anthrōpos estin)
readings.en: and it is human
readings.plain: it is human

why: The consonants 'nsh can be read 'anush 'incurable' (the Masoretic vowels, as in 15:18; 30:12) or 'enosh 'a human being', which is what the Greek read. 4QJer-a writes the word without a vowel letter, so it cannot decide. The Plain English Translation follows 'incurable', the sense that fits the sickness image of the surrounding chapters.

a: the gate of the people's sons
t: 'The people' with or without the article
p: The written text and a Qumran copy have 'people' without 'the'; the Masoretic reading adds it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (Qere, the reading marked in the margin)
readings.en: the sons of the people
readings.plain: the gate of the people's sons

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Ketiv, the written text); 4QJer-a (4Q70), about 200-150 BC, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss)
readings.en: the sons of a people
readings.plain: the gate of the people's sons

why: The difference is only the article, and the English reads the same either way. The scroll's 'the kings of Judah' later in the verse agrees with the Masoretic Text and the Greek (the transcription runs two words together). The Greek has 'the gates of the sons of your people'. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic reading.

a: let us give no heed to any of his words
t: Ignore him, or listen to him?
p: The Greek has 'we will listen to all his words'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70), about 200-150 BC, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss) (the word 'and not' is visible)
readings.en: and let us not pay attention to any of his words
readings.plain: let us give no heed to any of his words

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (akousometha pantas tous logous autou)
readings.en: and we will hear all his words
readings.plain: let us listen to all his words

why: The Greek reads without the negative. The scroll shows the negative, as the Masoretic Text does. The Plain English Translation follows them. The Greek's reading, 'strike him with the tongue and hear all his words', might mean they will gather evidence against him, but the Hebrew sense is clear.

a: listen to the voice of those who argue against me
t: 'My opponents', 'the words of my opponents' or 'my plea'?
p: Three forms of one phrase.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the voice of my opponents
readings.plain: listen to the voice of those who argue against me

readings.w: 4QJer-a (4Q70), about 200-150 BC, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss)
readings.en: the voice of the words of my opponents
readings.plain: listen to the words of those who argue against me

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (tou dikaiōmatos mou)
readings.en: the voice of my just claim
readings.plain: listen to my plea for justice

why: The scroll appears to add 'words of' ('to the voice of the words of my opponents'). The Greek read the consonants of 'my opponents' (yeriyvay) as 'my cause, my suit' (riyvi), which suits a lawsuit prayer. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text.

a: as burnt offerings to Baal
t: 'As burnt offerings to Baal': not in the Greek
p: The Greek ends the clause at 'in the fire'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: burnt offerings to Baal
readings.plain: as burnt offerings to Baal

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: The Greek lacks the phrase. It can be a later explanation in the Hebrew (comparing 7:31 and 32:35, where the god is not or is Molech) or a short text in the Greek. No scroll preserves 19:5. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: People will bury the dead in Topheth for lack of room anywhere else.
t: Burying in Topheth: not in the Greek
p: The Greek lacks the last sentence of verse 11.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and in Topheth they will bury, for lack of room to bury
readings.plain: People will bury the dead in Topheth for lack of room anywhere else.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus

why: The sentence repeats 7:32, where the Hebrew has it too. The Greek lacks it here. 4QJer-c preserves part of 19:8-9 but not this verse. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: Terror all around
p: The Greek gives Pashhur's new name as 'Exile', with no 'all around'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-c (4Q72), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss) (preserves 'magor', the 'all around' is restored)
readings.en: Terror all around
readings.plain: Terror all around

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (metoikon)
readings.en: Exile (sojourn)
readings.plain: Exile

why: The Greek translated magor as 'sojourning, exile' (the sense of the same letters in Genesis 17:8; 28:4), which matches the Greek of 20:4 ('I give you to exile'). Hebrew magor can also mean 'terror' (as in Psalm 31:13), and Jeremiah's own use of the phrase in 6:25 and 20:10 shows he meant terror. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: a terror, to yourself and to all your friends
p: The Greek again has 'exile'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QJer-c (4Q72), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss) (the scroll has the word magor but without the prefix 'to')
readings.en: a terror to you and to all your friends
readings.plain: a terror, to yourself and to all your friends

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (eis metoikian ... sun pasi tois philois sou)
readings.en: to exile, with all your friends
readings.plain: an exile, you and all your friends

why: See the entry on 20:3. The scroll has the same word, magor, but writes it without the prefix lamed that the Masoretic Text has (lemagor), which does not change the sense. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: the reward of his ways
p: The written text has 'his way'; the margin reads 'his ways'; the Plain English Translation follows the margin.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (Qere, the reading marked in the margin)
readings.en: according to his ways
readings.plain: the reward of his ways

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Ketiv, the written text); 4QJer-a (4Q70), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss) (spelled with a final waw only)
readings.en: according to his way
readings.plain: the reward of his way

why: The difference is one letter and hardly changes the sense. The scroll's spelling is the Ketiv's, though a spelling without the plural yod can also stand for a plural. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere.

a: Those who turn away from me
t: Who turns away: a vowel question
p: The written and the read forms of one word differ in their vowels.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (pointed reading)
readings.en: those who turn away from me
readings.plain: Those who turn away from me

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Ketiv, the written form, as recorded in the ETCBC data)
readings.en: my departers
readings.plain: my departers

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition from Codex Vaticanus (aphestekotes epi tes ges)
readings.en: those who stand away on the earth
readings.plain: those who stand away on the earth

why: Both Hebrew forms come from the root swr, 'turn aside'; they differ in vowels and doubling, not in a letter. The Greek has no 'from me', so the first-person shift of the Hebrew (in a verse that otherwise speaks to the LORD) is not there. The Plain English Translation follows the pointed Hebrew and keeps 'from me'.
